reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a forex robot or arbitrage software with a stated profit of $27,302 and directs viewers to an associated Telegram group. Trading-platform screens repeat the 2,726 percent and $27,302 figures alongside WesternPips.com, connecting the return claim to the promoted software destination. the available video evidence does not establish that the results are genuine, representative, or guaranteed, or that viewers had to pay, transfer funds, or provide data.

citations.quote: Join our new group in telegram

opening.argument: The evidence does not contain a promise that any viewer will receive these results, a guarantee of future performance, or an instruction to surrender funds. The title identifies a forex robot and latency-arbitrage subject, while the description identifies software and a Telegram group, but neither text says that participation is risk-free or that the displayed outcome is assured. The frames show a trading-platform presentation of a reported result alongside the website, not language promising the same result to every viewer. That distinction matters: displaying a performance figure can be an example or record without being a guarantee.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution treats the number as a solicitation by association. But its own evidence establishes only that a figure appears with software branding and a group invitation. It does not establish that the figure was promised to viewers, that future returns were represented as certain, or that viewers were told to deposit money. The absence of those essential terms leaves a reasonable non-scam reading: a presentation of a trading tool and an account result whose risks and validity require independent evaluation.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The displayed language is not neutral risk disclosure: it prominently pairs “PROFIT: +2 726 %” and “27 302 $” with the promoted site. The title likewise combines “Forex Robot” with “Profit,” and the description explicitly names “Arbitrage Trading Software.” A formal guarantee is unnecessary when extraordinary returns are presented as the central promotional message. The evidence does not need to prove a deposit instruction to show that the promotion invites belief in a profitable system.

opening.argument: A grounded reading is that this is a technology demonstration or performance display, not proof of a deceptive solicitation. The title focuses on a forex robot and latency arbitrage, and the description calls the offering “Arbitrage Trading Software.” The repeated trading-platform screens show account history, orders, charts, and a displayed result associated with the site. Those are the materials one would expect when demonstrating an automated trading tool or showing how it operated. Nothing supplied identifies a speaker making a personal promise, tells viewers that the result is typical, or states that viewers must buy or fund an account.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the presentation a demonstration is not speculative: the supplied frames visibly consist of trading interfaces, charts, order records, and account-history material. The prosecution offers no quotation of an inducement, payment demand, or guaranteed outcome. The website and Telegram references can identify the tool or its community without converting every demonstration of software into a scam. The proper conclusion is that the content shows a trading-system example whose claims remain unverified, not that deception is established.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The operational screens do not make the message educational. They repeatedly overlay the same extraordinary return figures and the promoted domain, while the title calls the subject a “Profit” robot and the description supplies a Telegram destination. No tutorial steps, technical explanation, testing method, limitations, or cautionary analysis is shown in the supplied evidence. The most direct reading is promotion of the software through an apparent success result, not neutral instruction.

opening.argument: Even accepting that the content promotes something, the supplied material fits ordinary software or service promotion more closely than a demonstrated scam mechanism. The description gives a software description, a website, an email address, and communication channels, but it does not request credentials, a deposit, a transfer, or trading authorization. The frames show trading records and a site name, yet do not show a payment page, account-access request, downline structure, or guaranteed-income instruction. A profit figure may be marketing for a trading product, but the evidence does not establish the transaction or deception needed to call it a scam.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution expressly concedes that the evidence does not establish a required deposit, transfer, data request, or trading permission. That concession is decisive against treating the item as a demonstrated scam mechanism. A website, email, Skype ID, and Telegram group are ordinary contact routes for a software service. The record shows a claimed result and a product reference, but not how a viewer would be defrauded or what payment is demanded.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A scam classification does not require the video to display a payment form or explicitly demand a deposit. The relevant evidence is the combination of a forex robot, an extraordinary profit claim, software branding, and a Telegram invitation. The description directs viewers toward the promoted ecosystem, while the frames repeatedly place the claimed return beside the site. Ordinary contact details do not neutralize a marketing claim whose authenticity and representativeness are unsupported.
